source_title: Statewide FAA-compliance requirement, penalty, and municipal preemption
regulated_party: Any person operating a qualifying UAV or UAS in Rhode Island
regulated_activity: Flying, piloting, controlling, directing, or programming a qualifying UAS
requirement_type: FAA-compliance mandate, misdemeanor exposure, and municipal preemption
permit_or_approval_required: No separate general state permit created; applicable FAA approvals remain required
summary: Rhode Island requires every operation of a qualifying UAV or UAS in the state to comply with all applicable FAA requirements. The statute defines covered UAVs as powered, unmanned, remotely piloted or autonomous vehicles weighing less than 55 pounds, and exempts operations under specified federal authority. A violation is subject to the misdemeanor penalty incorporated from § 1-4-19: a fine up to $500, imprisonment up to one year, or both. Municipalities may not enact or enforce UAS-operation ordinances except as otherwise authorized by FAA regulation or guidance or Rhode Island general law.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Use the state rule to identify what a political subdivision may regulate, then check only the controlling property's published operating terms before launch. Record the applicable boundary, property owner, designated-use area, notice, and permission status in the flight packet without assuming that state preemption eliminates property-use conditions.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Treat Statewide FAA-compliance requirement, penalty, and municipal preemption as a documented stop-work or redesign trigger because the packet identifies criminal, civil, evidentiary, or damage exposure. The contract and flight record should preserve the site screening, authority or exception relied upon, crew briefing, and incident/escalation path; obtain counsel where the facts sit near an undefined boundary or intent element.
notes: Definitions are at https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE1/1-8/1-8-1.1.htm. The incorporated penalty is at https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE1/1-4/1-4-19.htm.

regulated_party: Civil UAS owners and operators in Rhode Island
requirement_type: Compliance with federal UAS statutes, rules, and regulations
permit_or_approval_required: Only the federal approvals applicable to the operation are stated in the UAS-specific section
summary: The active Rhode Island Airport Corporation Aeronautics Regulations apply to civil aircraft operations and expressly define an unmanned aircraft as an aircraft operated without direct human intervention from within or on it. Section 1.17 requires all UAS operations to comply with federal statutes, rules, and regulations, including Part 107. RIAC may issue orders and take other authorized action to enforce the regulation and applicable Rhode Island aeronautics law. The current UAS-specific section does not state a separate RIAC flight permit, inspection-on-request duty, or operational checklist; those provisions appeared in older versions but were removed by the 2025 amendment.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Add Current Aeronautics Regulations UAS provision to the mission-specific legal and site screening for Statewide civil UAS operations. Brief the crew on the triggering conduct and document the operational boundary or exception relied upon before launch.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Preserve the mission screening and factual basis for compliance with 800-RICR-10-00-1 §§ 1.2, 1.4(35)-(36), 1.17, 1.19, including the operating area, purpose, approvals, and any relied-upon exception. Escalate ambiguous scope, conflicting client direction, or facts that could change the regulated party or activity before flight.
notes: The active amendment is effective January 29, 2025. Superseded 2018 and 2022 rule versions were reviewed only to confirm that their additional UAS subsections are no longer current.

source_title: State registration of federal aircraft certificates
status: Current / in force; UAS application mechanics unresolved
uas_topic: State aircraft registration; commercial operation; fees
regulated_party: Aircraft owners and operators based or primarily used in Rhode Island, and specified nonresident operators
regulated_activity: Registering federal aircraft certificates with RIAC while operating in Rhode Island
requirement_type: Annual state registration of federal aircraft certificates
permit_or_approval_required: RIAC registration; published fee is $30 for aircraft under 2,000 pounds
summary: Section 1-4-6 requires owners and operators of all aircraft based or primarily used in Rhode Island to register their federal aircraft certificates with RIAC, and states that nonresidents operating commercially intrastate shall register. The annual fee for aircraft under 2,000 pounds is $30. The active RIAC rule defines unmanned aircraft as aircraft and directs covered owners and operators to submit the federal registration certificate, annual application, and fee. However, the rule and current published application use conventional-aircraft terms such as N-number and airworthiness or experimental certificate, leaving the exact filing and onboard-document mechanics for ordinary Part 107 small UAS unresolved.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat the applicable written consent or authorization under R.I. Gen. Laws § 1-4-6; 800-RICR-10-00-1 §§ 1.4(2), 1.4(35), 1.5, 1.9(B) as a pre-mobilization gate and ensure it covers the site, dates, aircraft, crew, payload, and purpose. Do not lock the field schedule until the approving person and any notice, boundary, insurance, or operating conditions are documented.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Use the current Rhode Island application or request channel and provide pilot credentials, aircraft details, the current fee. The packet identifies the approval as: RIAC registration; published fee is $30 for aircraft under 2,000 pounds. Because the verified source does not establish a dependable review time for every case, confirm completeness, reviewer, lead time, approval duration, and field-contact expectations directly with the agency.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Maintain asset-level records for registration status, weight with each payload, serial number, airworthiness documents when applicable, and renewal dates before assigning an aircraft to this state. Fleet planning should account for fees, renewal lead time, and whether swapping an aircraft or payload changes the approval or registration basis.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the current application, all attachments, written approval, conditions, amendments, and closeout records under R.I. Gen. Laws § 1-4-6; 800-RICR-10-00-1 §§ 1.4(2), 1.4(35), 1.5, 1.9(B); a client's verbal direction should not substitute for the named authority's authorization. Escalate if the approving official, property boundary, operating dates, data rights, insurance terms, or ability to use a contractor is unclear.
verification_status: Verified authority; UAS-specific administrative mechanics unresolved
notes: RIAC rule: https://rules.sos.ri.gov/regulations/part/800-10-00-1. Current aircraft-registration instructions and form were reviewed; their fields remain tailored to conventional aircraft. Confirm the process directly with RIAC before relying on an exemption or submitting a small-UAS fleet.

summary: RIDEM rules allow UAS operation on, over, or from a public reservation only with official written permission from the public reservation manager and prohibit using UAS to harass or disturb users, wildlife, or natural resources. A violation may be fined up to $100 for each violation. Rhode Island State Parks lists drone use as a special-use activity requiring a permit and restricts approval to commercial use. Applicants must first contact the relevant regional or park office; ordinary applications are due at least 30 business days in advance, large activities may require 90 days to one year, and final approval can depend on insurance and activity-specific conditions.
